intro:
You have probably been burned before, or you know an owner who has. An agency promises the moon, takes a setup fee and a monthly retainer, posts a few pretty photos, and three months later your dining room is just as quiet on a Tuesday. Worse, you cannot even log into your own Instagram, because they set it up under their account and not yours.

Choosing the right marketing partner is one of the highest-stakes decisions you will make for your restaurant, and most owners walk in with no way to tell a real pro from a smooth talker. The good news is that you do not need to become a marketing expert to pick well. You just need to ask the right questions and know what a good answer sounds like.

This guide gives you ten specific questions to ask any Miami restaurant marketing agency before you sign anything. For each one, it tells you why it matters, what a strong answer sounds like, and the red-flag answer that should make you pause. We will walk through it step by step, question by question, so you can sit across from any agency and know exactly what to listen for.

sections.h2: Why the right agency matters more than the lowest price
sections.html:
When you compare agencies, the price is the easiest thing to look at, so it is tempting to just pick the cheapest one. Resist that. The real cost of a marketing agency is not the monthly fee. It is the months you lose, and the guests who never walked in, when the work is wrong.

Think about it in your own terms. If an agency charges a modest monthly fee but posts content nobody engages with, runs ads to the wrong people, and lets your Google listing go stale, you are not saving money. You are paying every month for something that does nothing, plus the sales you missed while a better partner would have been filling tables. A slightly pricier agency that actually books you covers pays for itself many times over.

The flip side is true too. The most expensive agency in Brickell is not automatically the best one for a family-run spot in Hialeah or Little Havana. Price tells you almost nothing about fit. What tells you about fit is how they answer the questions in this guide. So set a realistic budget, then judge every agency on their answers, not their rate card.

sections.h2: Get clear on your goal and budget before you call anyone
sections.html:
Before you talk to a single agency, spend twenty minutes getting clear on three things. Walking in with these makes you a sharper buyer and helps a good agency give you a straight answer instead of a generic pitch.

1. Your main goal

Pick the one outcome that matters most right now. More walk-ins on slow weeknights? A busier lunch crowd from the Brickell offices nearby? More catering and private-party bookings? Filling seats through the slower summer after tourist season winds down in the spring? An agency that hears a specific goal can build a specific plan. If you say you just want more marketing, you will get a generic package.

2. A realistic budget range

You do not need an exact number, just a range you are comfortable testing for a few months. Marketing is not a one-time purchase, it is an ongoing investment, so think in terms of a monthly amount. If you have no idea what is normal for a restaurant in this market, we broke down real numbers in our guide to what restaurant marketing costs in Miami. Read it first so no agency can quote you a random figure with a straight face.

3. Who your guests are

Jot down who actually eats with you: neighborhood regulars, tourists, office workers, families, a mostly Spanish-speaking crowd, or a mix. The more clearly you can describe your guests, the faster you will spot an agency that gets your market versus one that treats every restaurant the same.

sections.h2: Questions 1 to 5: track record, team, and what you are paying for
sections.html:
Here are the first five questions, in the order I would ask them. For each one, I have written what a good answer sounds like and what a red-flag answer sounds like, so you can tell the difference in real time.

1. Can you show me results from other restaurants like mine?

Why it matters: Anyone can say they get results. Real proof is specific: a named restaurant, what changed, and over what time. You want to see they have done this for a place like yours, not just an online store or a dentist's office.

A good answer sounds like: 'Here is a taqueria in Doral we helped. Their weekday orders grew over four months, and here is the owner's number if you want to ask them yourself.' Specific numbers, real names, references you can actually call.

A red-flag answer sounds like: Vague brags with no names, screenshots of follower counts with nothing tied to sales, or 'we cannot share client details' for every single example. Followers are not covers served.

2. Who actually does the work day to day?

Why it matters: Many agencies sell you with their most senior person, then hand your account to a junior you never met. You deserve to know who is really posting, replying to reviews, and running your ads.

A good answer sounds like: 'Your account manager will be Maria. She looks after about eight restaurants, she is your main contact, and here is who does the design and the ad work behind her.' Real names and a clear point of contact.

A red-flag answer sounds like: They dodge the question, or it is always 'the team' with no one you can email directly. If you cannot get a name before you sign, you will not get one after.

3. Do you specialize in restaurants and hospitality?

Why it matters: Restaurants are their own world. Photographing food, timing posts around service, handling reservations and reviews, and marketing around tourist season are nothing like selling software. An agency that lives in hospitality already understands your problems.

A good answer sounds like: 'Most of our clients are restaurants, bars, and cafes. Here is how we handle a slow Tuesday, a new menu launch, and the December to April rush.' They speak your language without you explaining it.

A red-flag answer sounds like: 'We work with every kind of business.' A generalist can be fine for some tasks, but for a restaurant you usually want someone who has done it many times and knows the seasonal rhythm of a city like Miami.

4. Is there a long contract or lock-in?

Why it matters: A long contract protects the agency, not you. If they are confident in their work, they should be willing to earn your business month to month, or at least not trap you for a year if things go sideways.

A good answer sounds like: 'We work month to month after a short initial period, and you can cancel with thirty days notice.' Or a short, clearly explained term with an easy exit.

A red-flag answer sounds like: A twelve-month lock-in with a steep cancellation penalty, pushed hard on day one. Be extra careful if that long contract is paired with vague deliverables. That combination is how owners end up paying for nothing for a year.

5. What exactly is included each month, and what costs extra?

Why it matters: 'Social media management' can mean twelve posts a month or it can mean four. You need to know exactly what you get each month and what costs extra, so there are no surprise invoices and no letdowns.

A good answer sounds like: A simple written list. 'Each month you get this many posts and reels, review replies, and one promotion. Ad budget, photo shoots, and website changes are separate, and here is what those cost.' Clear scope, in writing.

A red-flag answer sounds like: 'We handle everything, do not worry about it.' Vague scope is where trust breaks down. If they cannot put it in a short written list, you cannot hold them to it.

sections.h2: Questions 6 to 10: reporting, response time, ownership, and pricing
sections.html:
These last five questions are the ones owners forget most often, and they are usually the ones that hurt later. Ask them all before you sign.

6. How and how often do you report results?

Why it matters: If you cannot see what the agency is doing and whether it is working, you are flying blind. Good agencies report in plain language and tie their work back to things you care about, like calls, reservations, direction requests, and orders, not just likes.

A good answer sounds like: 'You get a simple monthly report, and we hop on a short call to walk you through it. We track calls, direction requests, reservations, and orders where we can, not just follower growth.' Plain numbers you understand.

A red-flag answer sounds like: No regular reporting, or reports stuffed with impressions and follower counts and nothing tied to real business. If the only number that ever goes up is followers, ask what that has done for your covers.

7. How fast do you respond when something breaks?

Why it matters: In a restaurant, things break at the worst moments: a wrong menu link on a Friday night, a nasty review during a rush, an ad rejected right before a big weekend. You need to know how fast they answer when it counts.

A good answer sounds like: 'You can reach your account manager by text or email, and we respond the same day on weekdays, faster for anything urgent.' A clear promise and a real human to reach.

A red-flag answer sounds like: The only way to reach them is a ticket form, or they are already slow and vague during the sales process. If they are hard to reach while trying to win you, it only gets worse once they have you.

8. Do I own my accounts, content, and data if we part ways?

Why it matters: This is the one owners forget, and it is the most painful to learn the hard way. If the agency sets up your Instagram, your Google Business Profile, or your Facebook ad account under their own account, they can hold your pages, your followers, and your ad history hostage if you ever leave. You could lose years of work and reviews overnight.

A good answer sounds like: 'Everything is created under your accounts, in your name, on your email. You own it all. If we ever part ways, you keep your pages, your content, your ad account, and your data, and we simply remove ourselves.' Ownership starts and ends with you.

A red-flag answer sounds like: Any version of 'we manage all that on our end' without confirming that you are the owner. Insist that your Google Business Profile, your social pages, and your ad accounts are owned by you, on an email you control, before any work begins. Get it in writing.

9. Do you know the Miami market, and can you work in Spanish and English?

Why it matters: Miami is not a generic market. Your guests search and read reviews in both English and Spanish, tourist season runs roughly December to April, and a Wynwood crowd is not a Coral Gables crowd. An agency that knows the city and works in both languages reaches people a one-language, out-of-town agency simply misses.

A good answer sounds like: 'We are local, we work in English and Spanish, and we tailor content to your neighborhood and to the season.' Even better if they can show you bilingual posts and review replies they have handled.

A red-flag answer sounds like: They treat Spanish as an afterthought, or they clearly do not know the difference between marketing a spot in Brickell and one in Hialeah. In this city, missing the Spanish-speaking half of the neighborhood means missing half your business.

10. How is pricing structured, and what does a realistic first 90 days look like?

Why it matters: You want to understand how you are charged (a flat retainer, per service, or a percentage of ad spend) and what is realistic early on. Honest agencies set clear expectations. Marketing takes time, and anyone promising instant results is guessing or exaggerating.

A good answer sounds like: 'Here is our flat monthly fee and what it covers. In the first ninety days we fix the foundations, then build momentum. Expect setup and small wins early, with bigger results building over the following months.' Clear pricing, honest timeline. For a sense of what those numbers usually look like, our breakdown of restaurant marketing costs in Miami is a good yardstick.

A red-flag answer sounds like: 'We guarantee you will double your sales in thirty days.' Nobody can promise that, and the ones who do tend to vanish when it does not happen. Be wary of pricing you cannot get in writing, or a quote that changes every time you ask.

sections.h2: Green flags: signs you found the right agency
sections.html:
Some signals tell you an agency is the real thing. If you see most of these, you are probably in good hands.

  • They ask you more questions than you ask them. A good agency wants to understand your restaurant, your goals, and your guests before pitching anything.
  • They give plain, specific answers. No buzzword soup. They explain what they will do in words you understand.
  • They have real restaurant experience and can point to spots like yours, with references you can call.
  • They are comfortable being measured. They talk about real outcomes and report honestly, even when a month is slow.
  • They put scope and pricing in writing without you having to push for it.
  • They confirm you own everything from the start: your accounts, your content, and your data.
  • They work in your guests' languages and know your neighborhood, from Wynwood to Doral to Little Havana.
  • They are honest about timelines and never promise overnight miracles.

sections.h2: Red flags: reasons to walk away
sections.html:
Just as important, some signals should make you pause or walk away, no matter how good the sales pitch feels.

  • Guarantees of instant or specific results. 'We will double your sales in a month' is a promise nobody can keep. Honest partners set real expectations instead.
  • Vague pricing or scope. If you cannot get a clear list of what you get and what it costs in writing, expect surprise invoices and disappointment.
  • They own your accounts, not you. Any refusal to set up your pages and ad accounts in your name, on your email, is a dealbreaker. This is how agencies hold restaurants hostage.
  • All follower counts, no business results. If every report is about likes and followers and never about calls, covers, or orders, the work may look busy but do nothing for you.
  • Hard pressure and long lock-ins. A rush to sign a twelve-month contract today, with a steep penalty to leave, protects them, not you.
  • You cannot tell who does the work or reach a real person quickly. If they are hard to reach while courting you, it gets worse later.
  • They do not know Miami or brush off working in Spanish. In this market, that is a real gap, not a small one.

sections.h2: How to start small, test an agency, and make the final call
sections.html:
You do not have to bet everything on day one. The smartest way to judge an agency is to watch them work on something small before you commit to a long relationship.

Start with a small project or a short trial

Ask if they will start with a defined first project or a short, month-to-month trial. A single month of social posts, a Google Business Profile cleanup, or one ad campaign for a specific goal tells you more than any sales call. You get to see the quality, the communication, and whether they actually do what they said.

Watch how they treat the small stuff

During that trial, pay attention to the things that predict a good long-term partner. Do they respond quickly? Do they explain what they are doing in plain language? Is the work on brand and free of sloppy mistakes? Do they hit the dates they promised? How an agency handles a small project is exactly how they will handle your whole account.

Make the final call

When it is time to decide, set the price aside for a minute and line up the answers. The right agency gave you specific proof, named the person doing your work, offered a fair contract, put scope and pricing in writing, confirmed you own your accounts, knew your market and your languages, and set honest expectations. If one agency checks those boxes and another just felt like a smooth pitch, you already know.

faqs.q: How do I choose a restaurant marketing agency?
faqs.a: Start by getting clear on your main goal, a realistic monthly budget, and who your guests are. Then ask every agency the same set of questions: can they show results from restaurants like yours, who actually does the work day to day, do they specialize in restaurants, is there a long contract, what is included each month, how do they report results, and do you keep full ownership of your accounts and data. Compare their answers, not just their prices, and favor the agency that gives specific, honest, plain-language answers over the smoothest pitch.

faqs.q: What questions should I ask a marketing agency before signing a contract?
faqs.a: Ask ten things before you sign. One, can you show results from restaurants like mine? Two, who does the work day to day? Three, do you specialize in restaurants? Four, is there a long contract or lock-in? Five, what exactly is included each month and what costs extra? Six, how and how often do you report results? Seven, how fast do you respond when something breaks? Eight, do I own my accounts, content, and data if we part ways? Nine, do you know the Miami market and work in English and Spanish? Ten, how is pricing structured and what does a realistic first ninety days look like?

faqs.q: Should a restaurant marketing agency require a long-term contract?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, and you should be cautious of one. A long lock-in protects the agency more than it protects you. Many good agencies work month to month after a short initial period, or offer a short, clearly explained term with an easy exit. A hard push to sign a twelve-month contract on day one, especially with a big cancellation penalty and vague deliverables, is a red flag. If an agency is confident in its work, it should be willing to earn your business over time rather than trap you.

faqs.q: Who should own my restaurant's social media and Google accounts, me or the agency?
faqs.a: You should. Your Instagram, Facebook, Google Business Profile, and any ad accounts should be created in your name, on an email you control, with you as the owner. A good agency works as a manager on your accounts, not the owner of them. If an agency sets these up under its own account, it can hold your pages, followers, reviews, and ad history hostage if you ever leave. Confirm your ownership in writing before any work begins.

faqs.q: How much should a Miami restaurant expect to pay a marketing agency?
faqs.a: It depends on what you need, from basic social media management to full service with ad management and content production, so think in terms of a monthly investment rather than a one-time cost. Rather than guess, ask each agency for clear pricing in writing, and compare it against typical market rates before you decide. Our guide to what restaurant marketing costs in Miami breaks down real numbers, which gives you a baseline so no agency can quote you a random figure.

faqs.q: How can I tell if a marketing agency actually understands restaurants?
faqs.a: Ask them to walk you through situations only restaurant people know well: a slow Tuesday, a new menu launch, a bad review during a Friday rush, or marketing through Miami's December to April tourist season. An agency that specializes in restaurants will answer easily and in your language, and most of its clients will be restaurants, bars, and cafes. A generalist who works with every kind of business often struggles to speak to the specific rhythm of running a restaurant.

faqs.q: What are the biggest red flags when hiring a restaurant marketing agency?
faqs.a: The biggest red flags are guarantees of instant or specific results such as doubling your sales in thirty days, vague pricing or scope you cannot get in writing, refusing to set your accounts up in your own name so you keep ownership, reports built only on followers and likes instead of real business results, heavy pressure to sign a long contract with a steep exit penalty, and not being able to tell you who actually does your work or reach a real person quickly. Any one of these is reason to slow down and ask more questions.
